::: {#fig-10-vla-cross-attention-intent-lease fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Grounded intent pipeline architecture across the silicon boundary**: Physical AI system architecture partitioning high-capacity deliberative reasoning on the Application Processor (AP) from deterministic safety enforcement on the real-time Safety Microcontroller Unit (MCU). The AP processes multimodal streams (RGB-D vision, natural language prompts, proprioception) through the intent model, whose computed `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_intent_infer_str` inference sets its `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_intent_str` rate. The 3D cost field box stands for an optional producer family of the VoxPoser kind; the running machine's intent model emits a target pose directly. A producer-side ambiguity filter, which passes only a singleton calibrated prediction set ($|\ConformalPredictionSet| = 1$), rejects ambiguous hypotheses before sending a structured intent proposal over the board-level link into the MCU's own memory; the two processors share no memory. The MCU independently verifies evidence epochs, physical actuator ceilings, and braking stopping reserve before arming the lease timer, whose expiry stops the drives without any message from the application processor; the permission path runs at `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_permission_str`, and trajectory admission remains a separate check (synthesized from Huang et al. [-@huang2023voxposer], Ahn et al. [-@ahn2022saycan], and Gray [-@gray1989leases])." fig-alt="Block diagram split by a dashed vertical boundary. On the application processor side, image, instruction, and state boxes feed an intent model box labeled inference 336 ms, runs at 2 Hz, which feeds a 3D cost field box and then an ambiguity diamond. The no branch leads down to a grounding refusal box; the yes branch crosses the boundary on a board link labeled SPI and DMA with CRC, sequence, and expiry, into a dashed mailbox box in MCU SRAM. On the safety MCU side the mailbox feeds a permission path box labeled 1 kHz tick, which feeds joint drives and arms a lease timer above; a red dashed lease-expiry line runs from the timer to the joint drives."}
![](images/svg/fig10_vla_cross_attention_intent_lease.svg){width="100%"}
:::

The pipeline therefore spans two processors that share no memory (@fig-10-vla-cross-attention-intent-lease). Everything that can be wrong about meaning runs on the application processor, and everything that must hold regardless of meaning runs on the Safety MCU. Its `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_permission_str` permission loop arms a lease timer that drops authority without any message from the host. That separation buys independence only when memory access, bus timing, and fault containment are qualified in each of three domains:

- *Application Processor (AP Domain):* A general-purpose, non-real-time operating system executing on host CPUs and hardware accelerators runs the vision-language backbones and, in architectures that use them, 3D cost fields. If the conformal prediction set over candidate referents contains multiple entries (@eq-intent-conformal-set), an upstream filter halts execution with an ambiguity alert. When the prediction set yields a unique referent ($|\ConformalPredictionSet| = 1$), the AP serializes the candidate goal pose, requested wrench limits, and parent belief digest into a fixed-size, statically structured intent proposal.
- *Board-Level Transport Boundary:* The proposal packet crosses from the AP to the discrete safety MCU over an isolated board-level interconnect, such as a Serial Peripheral Interface (SPI) bus backed by Direct Memory Access (DMA). The MCU receiver copies the transmission into a dedicated staging mailbox within local SRAM. The communication channel is treated as untrusted. Embedded CRC-32 checksums, monotonically increasing sequence numbers, and strict hardware timeout limits detect frame corruption, packet loss, and transmission stalls. The protocol design must also account for worst-case bus latency, as the bus interface alone guarantees no real-time delivery bounds.
- *Safety Microcontroller Unit (MCU Domain):* Operating on a dedicated real-time core, a deterministic control loop evaluates the incoming proposal as an unverified request. The MCU checks the evidence timestamp against its internal monotonic clock, verifies workspace envelopes and joint reachability limits, and clamps requested forces and velocities to certified plant limits. Furthermore, the MCU verifies that a deceleration trajectory can execute safely within existing clearance margins. The MCU arms a hardware countdown timer to the lease expiry $\IntentLeaseExpiry$ only after the proposal passes all admission gates. The expiry is the earliest of evidence decay, host silence, and the stopping deadline (@sec-intent-lease formalizes it). The MCU then grants bounded tracking authority to the joint drives.

### What each proposal family leaves to admission {#sec-intent-proposal-families}

This three-domain boundary stays fixed even when the upstream grounding model is swapped for a different proposal family. What changes from one model family to the next is which physical checks remain for admission to supply. An upstream model may emit a 2D bounding box, a 3D cost field, a scored 6-DoF grasp, or a chunk of normalized action tokens. In every case, treating that output directly as a motion command skips the physical checks that prevent an unseen obstacle collision, a joint-limit hit, or an unbraked contact impact. The pipeline's stages draw on multimodal feature extraction, cross-attention alignment, and open-vocabulary phrase grounding from computer vision and natural language processing [@kamath2021mdetr; @gu2022open; @radford2021learning; @liu2023grounding], yet an embodied machine cannot rely on a model's internal activations for physical safety. For example, a semantic skill ranker like SayCan outputs a discrete skill identifier scored by language affordance and value functions [@ahn2022saycan]. A programmatic generator like Code as Policies produces a control script that calls perception and motion APIs [@liang2023code]. VoxPoser synthesizes 3D spatial value maps (@fig-10-value-map-composition). OK-Robot emits a distribution of sampled grasp poses (@fig-10-real-open-vocab-grounding). Because none of these outputs natively carries a bounded wrench envelope, a certified clearance margin, or a hardware lease expiration, choosing one model family over another only shifts where conversion happens and leaves the admission checks in @tbl-10-grounding-paradigms unchanged.

Predicting a syntactically valid coordinate or control script never guarantees physical feasibility. Vision-language and action models are trained to maximize sequence likelihood over offline demonstration datasets. Their loss functions encode neither metric distances, rigid-body collision avoidance, manipulator Jacobian conditioning, nor frictional contact dynamics. Validating a candidate action requires deterministic physical checks evaluated within explicit coordinate frames. These checks include signed-distance queries over robot and environment meshes to verify clearance, numerical inverse-kinematics solvers with joint-limit and singularity screening, and Coulomb friction models to confirm that the planned grasp wrench resists expected gravitational and inertial loads. For contact-rich tasks such as sliding an object, turning a latch, or executing a handover, the system can simulate candidate trajectories in a rigid-body physics engine before committing actuator current. However, simulation fidelity remains bounded by the accuracy of estimated surface friction and inertial parameters. Downstream controllers must still enforce real-time admission checks regardless of simulation outcomes.

::: {#fig-10-value-map-composition fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Composing value maps for a grasp request**: An original schematic of the value-map interface introduced by VoxPoser [@huang2023voxposer], drawn on one horizontal slice of a voxel grid. (a) An affordance map rewards voxels near the handle the instruction names. (b) An avoidance map penalizes voxels near an observed obstacle. (c) The planner searches the composed cost for a path. The path is good only with respect to the maps: an obstacle the observations missed adds nothing to the avoidance map, so the path can run through it." fig-alt="Three heat maps of the same rectangular grid. Left: green shading, darkest around a star marking the handle. Middle: red shading, darkest around a small square marking an observed obstacle. Right: gray composed cost with a bronze path that runs from a dot on the left, arches over the dark obstacle region, and ends at the star, passing through a hollow red square labeled unobserved obstacle."}

```{python}
#| label: plot-intent-value-map-composition
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ VALUE-MAP COMPOSITION FOR A GRASP REQUEST (SCHEMATIC FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-10-value-map-composition
# │
# │ Goal:    teach the value-map interface (affordance + avoidance -> cost ->
# │          planner) and its blind spot, in an original drawing.
# │ Show:    three maps on one voxel slice and the planned path, which passes
# │          through an obstacle the observations missed.
# │ How:     schematic fields on a unitless grid; Dijkstra on the composed cost.
# │          No physical quantity is drawn.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import heapq
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from mlsysim import viz

# ┌── 1. LOAD: a schematic tabletop slice (no physical claim) ───────────────
NX, NY = 60, 36  # voxel columns and rows in the drawn slice  # category: illustrative (drawing)
START = (4, 18)  # gripper voxel  # category: illustrative (drawing)
TARGET = (52, 22)  # handle voxel named by the instruction  # category: illustrative (drawing)
OBSTACLE = (30, 17)  # voxel center of an observed obstacle  # category: illustrative (drawing)
SIGMA_OBS = 5.0  # voxels, avoidance falloff  # category: illustrative (drawing)
W_AVOID = 12.0  # weight of avoidance against affordance  # category: illustrative (drawing)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE: compose value maps, then plan on the composed cost ─────────
yy, xx = np.mgrid[0:NY, 0:NX]
dist_t = np.hypot(xx - TARGET[0], yy - TARGET[1])
affordance = np.exp(-dist_t / 18.0)  # high near the handle
avoidance = np.exp(-((xx - OBSTACLE[0]) ** 2 + (yy - OBSTACLE[1]) ** 2) / (2 * SIGMA_OBS**2))
cost = (1.0 - affordance) + W_AVOID * avoidance + 0.05

def _plan(c, s, g):
    """Dijkstra over 8-connected voxels; returns the voxel path from s to g."""
    best = {s: 0.0}
    prev = {}
    pq = [(0.0, s)]
    while pq:
        d, u = heapq.heappop(pq)
        if u == g:
            break
        if d > best.get(u, np.inf):
            continue
        for dx in (-1, 0, 1):
            for dy in (-1, 0, 1):
                v = (u[0] + dx, u[1] + dy)
                if (dx or dy) and 0 <= v[0] < NX and 0 <= v[1] < NY:
                    nd = d + np.hypot(dx, dy) * c[v[1], v[0]]
                    if nd < best.get(v, np.inf):
                        best[v] = nd
                        prev[v] = u
                        heapq.heappush(pq, (nd, v))
    path = [g]
    while path[-1] != s:
        path.append(prev[path[-1]])
    return np.array(path[::-1])

path = _plan(cost, START, TARGET)
UNSEEN = tuple(path[int(0.72 * len(path))])  # an obstacle the observations missed lies on the path

# ┌── 3. PLOT ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
viz.set_book_style()
C = viz.COLORS
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(6.3, 2.05))
panels = (
    (affordance, "Greens", "(a) affordance map"),
    (avoidance, "Reds", "(b) avoidance map"),
    (cost, "Greys", "(c) composed cost, planned path"),
)
for ax, (field, cmap, title) in zip(axes, panels):
    ax.imshow(field, origin="lower", cmap=cmap, interpolation="nearest", vmin=0, vmax=np.percentile(field, 99))
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=9, fontweight="normal", pad=4)
    ax.set_xticks([])
    ax.set_yticks([])
    ax.grid(False)
    ax.plot(*TARGET, marker="*", ms=9, color=viz.VOL4_ROLES["structural"], mec="white", mew=0.6, zorder=5)
    ax.plot(*OBSTACLE, marker="s", ms=6, color=viz.VOL4_ROLES["consequence"], mec="white", mew=0.6, zorder=5)
axes[0].text(
    TARGET[0],
    TARGET[1] - 5,
    "handle",
    fontsize=9,
    ha="center",
    va="top",
    color=C["primary"],
    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc="white", ec="none"),
)
axes[1].text(OBSTACLE[0], OBSTACLE[1] - 8, "observed\nobstacle", fontsize=9, ha="center", va="top", color=C["primary"])
ax = axes[2]
ax.plot(path[:, 0], path[:, 1], color=viz.VOL4_ROLES["proposal"], lw=1.8, zorder=4)
ax.plot(*START, marker="o", ms=5, color=viz.VOL4_ROLES["proposal"], zorder=5)
ax.plot(*UNSEEN, marker="s", ms=7, mfc="white", mec=viz.VOL4_ROLES["consequence"], mew=1.2, ls="none", zorder=5)
ax.annotate(
    "unobserved\nobstacle",
    xy=UNSEEN,
    xytext=(UNSEEN[0] + 1, UNSEEN[1] - 16),
    ha="left",
    va="top",
    fontsize=9,
    color=viz.VOL4_ROLES["consequence"],
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", lw=0.6, color=viz.VOL4_ROLES["consequence"]),
)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.01, right=0.99, top=0.88, bottom=0.02, wspace=0.06)
plt.show()
```

:::

In VoxPoser's value-map interface (@fig-10-value-map-composition), an affordance map rewards voxels near the handle the instruction names, an avoidance map penalizes voxels near observed obstacles, and the planner follows the composed cost around the obstacle it can see. Because the planned path is optimal only with respect to what the maps contain, an obstacle that the observations missed adds no cost and the path runs straight through it, leaving clearance against unobserved space to the permission path.

::: {#fig-10-real-open-vocab-grounding fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Open-vocabulary grasp grounding pipeline**: OK-Robot combines candidate grasp generation with language-conditioned object selection and geometric filtering [@liu2024okrobot]. An open-vocabulary detector isolates the target object mask, candidate grasps are sampled across the 3D point cloud, and geometric heuristics prune inadmissible approaches. The resulting grasp pose represents a candidate proposal; bounding tolerances, evidence deadlines, and independent permission checks are an architectural wrapper developed in this chapter. (Source: @liu2024okrobot, CC BY 4.0)." fig-alt="OK-Robot figure showing a robot camera view, candidate grasps, a language-conditioned target mask, filtering, and a selected grasp pose. The image illustrates proposal generation; it does not show a certified collision check or an expiring intent lease."}
![](images/jpg/fig10_real_open_vocab_grounding.jpg){width="95%"}
:::

OK-Robot shows the same division in a modular pipeline (@fig-10-real-open-vocab-grounding) [@liu2024okrobot]. Open-vocabulary detectors (OWL-ViT and SAM) isolate the queried object, a class-agnostic generator (AnyGrasp) samples dense 6-DoF candidates over the point cloud, and geometric heuristics prune them to a single pose. That pose is still an uncertified Stage 4 proposal. Before it can command joint motion, it must be bound to dated sensor evidence, given a wrench envelope, and admitted under an expiring lease on the Safety MCU. Every proposal family in @tbl-10-grounding-paradigms leaves a comparable residue, which the table's last column itemizes as the evidence admission must still supply.

| Proposal source           | Representation sent downstream                          | Early check                                                | Remaining evidence needed                                                                              |
|:--------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 2D box or mask            | Image region plus measured depth and camera calibration | Reject absent depth or a target outside a validated region | 3D pose error, occlusion, object identity, and swept-path clearance                                    |
| 3D feature or value field | Candidate target or cost field in a stated frame        | Reject out-of-workspace targets and stale map cells        | Conservative occupancy, unknown-space policy, actuator and timing bounds                               |
| Action VLA                | Decoded action or action chunk in its trained range     | Reject out-of-range or inadmissible proposals              | State-dependent physical limit and independent permission; the action head provides no clearance proof |
| Learned grasp generator   | Set of 6-DoF grasp poses with learned scores            | Reject grasps outside the workspace or jaw aperture        | Measured success on this gripper, IK and joint limits, approach clearance, and wrench capacity         |
| Language-selected skill   | Skill identifier with estimated success                 | Rank or decline low-confidence candidates                  | Current preconditions, path feasibility, and separate physical enforcement                             |

: **Grounding representations and admission questions**: Outputs from different model families require different conversions before a physical permission check. {#tbl-10-grounding-paradigms tbl-colwidths="[18,24,24,34]"}

```{python}
#| label: calc-intent-state-of-practice
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
# │ Literature values quoted beside the state-of-practice table.               │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
class StateOfPractice:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    n_action_bins = 256  # category: literature (Brohan et al. 2023, RT-1; Kim et al. 2024, OpenVLA)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(n_action_bins == 2**8, "Uniform action bins fit one byte per dimension")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    n_bins_str = fmt_int(n_action_bins)
```

Regardless of the specific output architecture, raw actions generated by VLA models carry no certified metric bounds. These heads normalize action spaces relative to empirical training distributions rather than physical workspace obstacles. For example, RT-1 and OpenVLA discretize each continuous action dimension into `{python} StateOfPractice.n_bins_str` uniform bins across bounded ranges [@brohan2023rt1; @kim2024openvla]. FAST tokenizes the discrete cosine transform coefficients of a multi-step trajectory chunk [@pertsch2025fast]. In contrast, $\pi_0$ generates continuous action chunks through a flow-matching diffusion expert, predicting `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.pi0_chunk_str` steps per inference and streaming them at up to `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.pi0_rate_str` [@black2024pi0]. Although each approach outputs kinematically coherent trajectories within its training distribution, none verifies dynamic feasibility or collision clearance against surrounding obstacles. Similarly, spatial location tokens in vision-language models like PaliGemma quantize normalized pixel coordinates on the camera sensor. These image tokens transform into metric poses only after incorporating measured depth maps, camera intrinsics, and hand-eye calibration matrices. The geometric uncertainty propagated through this calibration chain, particularly along the camera's optical axis, often dwarfs the discretization error of the underlying token grid.

@Tbl-10-grounding-paradigms sorts proposals by the representation they send downstream, a classification that outlasts any one model. The systems that fill each role change within a few years, so @tbl-10-state-of-practice dates them separately, pairing what each current system emits with what the permission path must still establish on its own.

| Role in the pipeline                 | Representative systems (year)               | What the system emits                                    | What the permission path must still establish           |
|:-------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|
| Open-vocabulary detection            | OWL-ViT (2022), Grounding DINO (2023)       | Boxes with independent per-box text scores               | Uniqueness, depth, and object identity                  |
| Promptable segmentation and tracking | SAM 2 (2024)                                | Object masks propagated through video                    | The tracker's own error and latency bounds              |
| Learned grasp generation             | Contact-GraspNet (2021), AnyGrasp (2023)    | Scored 6-DoF grasp sets                                  | IK, aperture, clearance, and wrench capacity            |
| Language to symbolic plan            | LLM+P (2023)                                | A PDDL problem solved by a classical planner             | Every geometric precondition                            |
| Calibrated request for help          | KnowNo (2023)                               | A conformal prediction set over options                  | Coverage under distribution shift; physical singulation |
| VLA action heads                     | OpenVLA (2024), $\pi_0$ (2024), FAST (2025) | Binned tokens, flow-matched chunks, or compressed tokens | Clearance, timing, and effort bounds                    |

: **State of practice for grounded intent, as of 2026**: Representative published systems for each pipeline role [@minderer2022simple; @liu2023grounding; @ravi2024sam2; @sundermeyer2021contactgraspnet; @fang2023anygrasp; @liu2023llmp; @ren2023robots; @kim2024openvla; @black2024pi0; @pertsch2025fast]. The required validation checks in the rightmost column remain architectural invariants even as specific model architectures are refreshed. {#tbl-10-state-of-practice tbl-colwidths="[20,24,26,30]"}

Every row leaves admission the same two questions, whether the metric estimate is tight enough for the task and whether it belongs to the right object. The mug's handle shows how each can fail while the other holds.

### Imprecise estimates and wrong objects {#sec-intent-estimate-identity}

```{python}
#| label: calc-intent-handle-ellipsoid
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
# │ The mug-handle localization estimate as a 95 percent region, compared with  │
# │ the mug's grasp tolerance axis by axis.                                     │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
import math

class HandleEllipsoid:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD: illustrative single-view localization model ────────────────────
    sigma_lat_x = 4.0 * millimeter  # category: illustrative (distant pre-approach wrist-camera view, lateral std. dev.)
    sigma_lat_y = 5.0 * millimeter  # category: illustrative (wrist-camera lateral std. dev.)
    sigma_depth = 12.0 * millimeter  # category: illustrative (wrist-camera depth std. dev.)
    chi2_3dof_95 = 7.815  # category: constant (chi-square quantile, 3 degrees of freedom, 0.95)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE: principal semi-axes of the 95 percent region ────────────────
    k_region = math.sqrt(chi2_3dof_95)
    semi_x = (k_region * sigma_lat_x).to(millimeter)
    semi_y = (k_region * sigma_lat_y).to(millimeter)
    semi_z = (k_region * sigma_depth).to(millimeter)
    chi2_cdf = math.erf(math.sqrt(chi2_3dof_95 / 2)) - math.sqrt(2 * chi2_3dof_95 / math.pi) * math.exp(-chi2_3dof_95 / 2)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD: the claims the prose makes ────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(chi2_cdf - 0.95) < 1e-4, "7.815 is the 0.95 chi-square quantile for 3 degrees of freedom")
    check(semi_x < AISLE.grasp_tolerance and semi_y < AISLE.grasp_tolerance, "Lateral semi-axes fit the grasp tolerance")
    check(semi_z > AISLE.grasp_tolerance, "Depth semi-axis exceeds the grasp tolerance")
    check(AISLE.grasp_initial_error < AISLE.grasp_tolerance, "Admitted handle estimate fits the tolerance")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT: rendered values ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    sigma_x_str = fmt_length(sigma_lat_x, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    sigma_y_str = fmt_length(sigma_lat_y, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    sigma_z_str = fmt_length(sigma_depth, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    chi2_str = fmt(chi2_3dof_95, precision=3, commas=False)
    semi_x_str = fmt_length(semi_x, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    semi_y_str = fmt_length(semi_y, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    semi_z_str = fmt_length(semi_z, unit=millimeter, precision=1)

semi_x = HandleEllipsoid.semi_x
semi_z = HandleEllipsoid.semi_z
```

When the wrist camera views the red mug from across the workstation before the arm begins its reach, depth uncertainty along the optical ray stretches the 95 percent error region to more than twice the handle's grasp tolerance. Closing the gripper on that single-frame estimate can therefore drive the fingers into the ceramic rim. Under an illustrative calibrated Gaussian sensor model for that pre-approach wrist-camera frame, the principal standard deviations in the camera frame are `{python} HandleEllipsoid.sigma_x_str` and `{python} HandleEllipsoid.sigma_y_str` laterally, and `{python} HandleEllipsoid.sigma_z_str` along the optical depth axis. Because the optical axis aligns with the gripper's approach vector, range uncertainty directly challenges position control. A **95 percent statistical region** surrounding the estimated handle coordinate $\CartesianPosition_0$ is defined by the Mahalanobis squared distance $(\CartesianPosition-\CartesianPosition_0)^\top\PerceptionDepthCovariance^{-1}(\CartesianPosition-\CartesianPosition_0)\le\PositionConfidenceEllipsoidRadius^2$. With the three-degree-of-freedom chi-square quantile $\PositionConfidenceEllipsoidRadius^2 =$ `{python} HandleEllipsoid.chi2_str`, the distribution expands into principal semi-axes of `{python} HandleEllipsoid.semi_x_str`, `{python} HandleEllipsoid.semi_y_str`, and `{python} HandleEllipsoid.semi_z_str`.

Against the mug's `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.r_tol_str` physical grasp tolerance (@fig-10-intent-lease-envelope, panel a), the ellipsoid fails on one axis only. While both lateral semi-axes fall comfortably within the mechanical tolerance window, the depth semi-axis of `{python} HandleEllipsoid.semi_z_str` substantially exceeds the allowed threshold. Consequently, the admission gate rejects the proposal, because the controller cannot guarantee that closing the gripper fingers at that estimated setpoint will capture the handle rather than collide with the rim.

The remedy, worked through in @sec-intent-admissible-goal-sets, decomposes the reach into distinct phases. The system first admits an intermediate, collision-checked inspection waypoint, allowing the arm to travel closer to the workspace. Once positioned nearby, a second wrist-camera observation constructs a refined belief record, reducing the initial position uncertainty to `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.e0_str`. Because a Gaussian probability region retains an unbounded asymptotic tail, statistical distributions alone cannot certify absolute spatial clearance. The downstream intent proposal therefore needs independently justified conservative error envelopes in the robot base frame before requesting trajectory tracking. Covariance alone supplies only a statistical region.

```{python}
#| label: calc-intent-envelope-figure
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SYNC GUARD FOR THE HAND-DRAWN TARGET AND LEASE-EXPIRY FIGURE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-10-intent-lease-envelope (SVG labels are hand-typed; panel (a)
# │          is drawn at 3 px/mm).
# │
# │ Goal:    Fail the build if a value the figure draws changes.
# │ Show:    lateral 11.2 mm and depth 33.5 mm semi-axes, 15 mm tolerance,
# │          22 ms drive onset after lease expiry.
# │ How:     Reads calc-intent-handle-ellipsoid and
# │          calc-intent-lease-duration-collision-exposure.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
check(round(semi_x.to(millimeter).magnitude, 1) == 11.2, "envelope figure: lateral semi-axis label is stale")
check(round(semi_z.to(millimeter).magnitude, 1) == 33.5, "envelope figure: depth semi-axis label is stale")
check(abs(AISLE.grasp_tolerance.to(millimeter).magnitude - 15.0) < 1e-9, "envelope figure: tolerance label is stale")
check(abs(t_arm_onset_after_expiry.to(millisecond).magnitude - 22.0) < 1e-9, "envelope figure: drive onset label is stale")
```

::: {#fig-10-intent-lease-envelope fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Localization uncertainty and authority expiry**: Panel (a) draws the handle estimate's 95 percent region to scale against the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.r_tol_str` grasp tolerance: the lateral semi-axis of `{python} HandleEllipsoid.semi_x_str` fits, while the `{python} HandleEllipsoid.semi_z_str` depth semi-axis along the camera ray does not. Panel (b) sketches speed against time: renewals keep the lease alive, and when they stop the lease expires, the drive takes `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_arm_onset_str` to begin braking, and a jerk-limited stop follows. The shaded area is the stopping distance, which must fit the clearance that remains; the dashed trace is motion with no lease, which never stops." fig-alt="Two panels. Left: a tall ellipse labeled 95 percent region, centered on point p0 below a wrist camera, overlaps a dashed square labeled tolerance 15 millimeters; the ellipse fits the square sideways, with a lateral dimension of 11.2 millimeters, but extends above and below it, with a depth dimension of 33.5 millimeters. Right: speed against time. A solid line at v max carries three renewal dots, then a red vertical line marks lease expiry, an amber band marks drive onset 22 milliseconds, and the line curves smoothly down to zero speed. The area under the falling part is shaded and labeled d stop equals the integral of v dt, at most the clearance left. A red dashed line continues at v max, labeled no lease, no stop. Brackets under the axis mark the admitted lease and the jerk-limited stop."}
![](images/svg/fig10_intent_lease_envelope.svg){width="100%"}
:::

While a configured statistical gate cleanly rejects detections with large variance envelopes, it cannot catch an entirely incorrect object identified with high semantic confidence. This is a different case from the jar beside the mug, where both candidates entered the prediction set and the producer refused. Consider instead the jar in place of the mug, where a fragile, thin-walled glass jar sits on the workstation where the ceramic mug was expected and no mug is present. When prompted to pick the mug, the vision-language model misidentifies the jar with strong semantic certainty, generating a sharp, low-variance geometric proposal centered on the glass container. The downstream trajectory planner accepts the coordinate, solves inverse kinematics in $\SpecialEuclideanGroup$, verifies joint position and velocity limits, and confirms that the approach path clears all static obstacles in the occupancy map. Because the requested motion satisfies all kinematic and wrench envelopes, the real-time permission path authorizes execution. However, if the gripper applies the clamping force required to hold a heavy ceramic mug, the jaws crush the thin glass container upon contact despite clearing every geometric check.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_wrong_object_chain.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Three dots joined by arrows: an orange dot labeled confident wrong object, a slate dot labeled passes geometric checks, and a red dot labeled mug-rated squeeze."}

*A confident wrong object passes every geometric check until the gripper closes.*
:::

This scenario marks the boundary between physical verification and semantic premises. The deterministic permission path enforces coordinate envelopes, kinematic limits, actuator torque thresholds, and obstacle clearance against known geometric occupancy grids. These physical invariants cannot confirm whether a given coordinate actually corresponds to the requested object. The premise that the targeted item is indeed the requested ceramic mug remains an unverified upstream assumption outside the hardware controller's reach. Establishing that premise requires distinct task-level perceptual evidence, which must be tracked through the handover release case (@sec-release-case-worked-full) and recorded in the residual-claims register (@sec-frontier-residual-claims-register). A learned task filter upstream cannot close this gap either. The AutoRT deployment showed that a language-model task filter improved the fraction of sensible task proposals while unsafe commands still passed it. Human teleoperators therefore had to intervene and halt execution (war story \ref{ws-intent-autort-hallucination-constitution}) [@ahn2023autort].

```{python}
#| label: calc-intent-autort-filter
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
# │ AutoRT task-filter counts (Ahn et al. 2024, Sec. 5.3): acceptable fractions │
# │ before and after the constitutional filter, and the filter's recall.        │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
class AutoRTFilter:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD: reported counts ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    n_total = 259  # category: literature (Ahn et al. 2024, tasks sampled)
    n_ok = 228  # category: literature (acceptable before filtering)
    n_kept = 214  # category: literature (kept by the filter)
    n_kept_ok = 200  # category: literature (acceptable among kept)
    n_bad = 31  # category: literature (unsuitable tasks in the sample)
    n_caught = 17  # category: literature (unsuitable tasks the filter rejected)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE: fractions and recall ────────────────────────────────────────
    n_missed = n_bad - n_caught
    pct_before = 100 * n_ok / n_total
    pct_after = 100 * n_kept_ok / n_kept
    recall = 100 * n_caught / n_bad

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(n_total - n_ok == n_bad, "Unsuitable count matches the sample")
    check(n_kept - n_kept_ok == n_missed, "Unsuitable tasks the filter kept match the misses")
    check(round(pct_before) == 88 and round(pct_after) == 93 and round(recall) == 55, "Reported percentages")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    n_total_str = fmt_int(n_total)
    n_ok_str = fmt_int(n_ok)
    n_kept_str = fmt_int(n_kept)
    n_kept_ok_str = fmt_int(n_kept_ok)
    n_bad_str = fmt_int(n_bad)
    n_caught_str = fmt_int(n_caught)
    n_missed_str = fmt_int(n_missed)
    pct_before_str = fmt_int(round(pct_before))
    pct_after_str = fmt_int(round(pct_after))
    recall_str = fmt_int(round(recall))
```

::: {#ws-intent-autort-hallucination-constitution .callout-war-story title="AutoRT task filtering and supervision (2024)"}
**Context**: AutoRT deployed foundation models to propose and filter physical manipulation tasks for fleets of mobile manipulators operating in unstructured human office environments [@ahn2023autort].

**Mechanism**: In a sample of `{python} AutoRTFilter.n_total_str` proposed tasks, human annotators judged `{python} AutoRTFilter.n_ok_str` (`{python} AutoRTFilter.pct_before_str` percent) acceptable. A second LLM pass then filtered the tasks against a robot "constitution" of safety and embodiment rules. Of the `{python} AutoRTFilter.n_kept_str` tasks it kept, `{python} AutoRTFilter.n_kept_ok_str` (`{python} AutoRTFilter.pct_after_str` percent) were acceptable. The filter rejected `{python} AutoRTFilter.n_caught_str` of the `{python} AutoRTFilter.n_bad_str` unsuitable tasks, a recall of `{python} AutoRTFilter.recall_str` percent, and passed the other `{python} AutoRTFilter.n_missed_str`.

**Impact**: All `{python} AutoRTFilter.n_missed_str` misses arose during teleoperated collection. Although the filter raised overall proposal quality, human supervisors had to intervene to intercept every unsafe proposal before robot execution.

**Response**: The system architecture placed physical safety outside the model's domain. Deployments supplemented learned proposals with hardware joint-force limits, physical emergency stop buttons, and direct human line-of-sight supervision or physical perimeter barricades.

**Systems lesson**: A learned task filter can improve proposal quality, but it cannot serve as a safety referee. An independent, deterministic permission and fallback path must validate every physical action against real-time plant limits before execution.
:::

The distant view and the glass jar mark two distinct verification boundaries. The distant view fails on metric uncertainty along the depth axis, whereas the jar in place of the mug fails on an unverified semantic premise, because metric precision does not establish object identity. A safe geometric proposal must therefore carry both dated physical evidence and task-specific selection evidence across the silicon boundary. By this point the mug proposal holds most of what the lease will carry. The grounded affordance has fixed the target pose and its goal region, and the squeeze bounds of the grasp analysis have set the wrench ceiling. The operator table has named the predicates the grasp must discharge, and the handle's error envelope has been compared with the task tolerance. Carrying these values is not yet holding authority, however. The proposal still lacks a grant, a deadline, and a stop that works without the proposer, and turning it into bounded authority over the arm is the work of the handoff.

## The Intent Handoff and Bounded Authority {#sec-intent-handoff}

If a deliberative host could stream raw joint trajectories or actuator currents directly to the drives, a two-millimeter depth error into a rigid latch plate or a stalled inference thread mid-reach would drive motor currents to saturation before any host process could intervene. When the arm reaches for the red mug, the deliberative host instead submits a candidate intent specifying a bounded target region, an expiration deadline, and explicit physical effort ceilings. The region and the ceilings are the grounding results packaged for transit, the affordance pose with its goal set and the grasp's wrench and speed limits, and the requested deadline is computed from the parent belief record's evidence epoch. An independent real-time supervisor intercepts this proposal, vetting each requested parameter against retained sensor evidence and configured plant dynamics. Granting a target lease merely authorizes downstream trajectory planning within certified safety bounds. The deliberative model remains isolated from low-level actuator registers.

This permission path validates every requested target constraint before any motion planner can generate trajectory setpoints. Rather than forcing memory-constrained microcontrollers to maintain full scene representations, host-side spatial engines export compact geometric evidence across a strictly typed interface. The supervisor verifies four mandatory invariants against this evidence:

1. *Spatial containment invariant:* The proposed geometric goal set $\GoalSet \subset \SpecialEuclideanGroup$ must lie strictly within the robot's reachable workspace manifold $\ReachableWorkspace$. The bounded spatial uncertainty envelope $(\XPositionErrorEnvelope, \YPositionErrorEnvelope, \ZPositionErrorEnvelope)$ must fit inside the task tolerance $(\XTaskToleranceSemiAxis, \YTaskToleranceSemiAxis, \ZTaskToleranceSemiAxis)$ without intersecting persistent obstacle geometry in spatial memory $\SpatialMemoryMap$.
2. *Temporal freshness invariant:* The sensor evidence epoch $\MonotonicClockInstant_0$ must match a retained parent belief record. The unobserved elapsed time on the Safety MCU's monotonic hardware clock must not exceed the evidence horizon $\EvidenceHorizon$ that @sec-intent-goals-expire takes from the parent belief record.
3. *Dynamic effort invariant:* Requested tool-center-point velocity $\SpeedBound$, acceleration $\ProfileAccelerationBound$, and contact wrench $\ContactWrenchCeiling = [\ContactForceCeiling, \ContactTorqueCeiling]^\top$ must remain strictly within actuator thermal ratings, link inertia limits, and workpiece structural yield thresholds.
4. *Certified deterministic fallback invariant:* The robot must possess an independently verified, pre-computed stopping or hold trajectory that brings all moving links to rest within current physical obstacle clearance ($\StoppingDistance \le \ClearDistance$) if authority is abruptly revoked.

The first three invariants turn the requirements that opened the chapter into checks: metric physicality and bounded error become spatial containment and the effort ceiling, while temporal expiration becomes freshness. The fourth adds the obligation those requirements left implicit, a stop that works without the proposer. Each invariant guards against a distinct failure mode in physical interaction. Loose target bounds can exceed kinematic grasp tolerances, and stale sensor evidence risks collision with a displaced object. Excessive commanded effort can shatter a workpiece, and an unvetted handoff leaves moving mass without a safe recovery trajectory. The resulting intent lease records the validated envelope that survives these four checks and constrains the downstream trajectory planner, which must synthesize path timing and deceleration profiles that satisfy supervisory admission criteria (@sec-intent-lease). Pairing the evidence epoch with a finite lease expiration\index{Intent record!temporal lease} keeps the temporal bound deterministic even if the host crashes, because the safety controller compares its own clock against the admitted deadline rather than waiting for a cancellation packet (@sec-intent-goals-expire).

Spatial and temporal bounds alone cannot guarantee safety if the downstream controller commands unbounded effort. Every intent proposal must therefore declare explicit effort ceilings\index{Intent record!force limits} covering tool-center-point velocity, acceleration, and contact wrench. Consider a depth perception error of two millimeters that places a target goal slightly inside a rigid workpiece. An unrestricted position controller will drive actuator currents to saturation trying to eliminate tracking error, imposing severe mechanical stress on the gear train. During a guarded approach to a spring-latched cage door, for example, the host proposes a `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_trip_str` tripwire ceiling, well below the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_lim_str` structural latch threshold, paired with an approach velocity capped at `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.v_latch_str`. The permission path evaluates these values against hardware torque-speed curves and environmental thresholds, admitting only parameters that guarantee structural integrity.

Downstream of the permission path, an impedance controller\index{Impedance controller} shapes interaction dynamics, answering a position error with the restoring force of the virtual spring-damper established in @sec-body-transmission-compliance [@hogan1985impedance]. Under quasi-static contact, scaling the virtual stiffness along the approach vector directly limits steady-state contact force for a given positional error. Transient impacts, however, demand more than static stiffness modulation; containing peak collision forces requires coordinating approach velocity, passive mechanical compliance, sensor latency, and actuator closed-loop bandwidth.

Omitting spatial, temporal, or dynamic boundaries leaves physical hardware vulnerable during communication dropouts or perception stalls. Stopping distance scales linearly with the reaction delay preceding brake engagement and quadratically with operating velocity (@eq-body-stopping-distance). For a mobile base navigating within physical obstacle clearances, a silent or stalled proposer inflates this reaction window by the entire lifespan of the active command lease. As established in @sec-nervous-lease-sizing, this chunk lease duration directly extends the unbraked latency parameter $\PrebrakeDelay$. The verified safety envelope must therefore maintain obstacle clearance greater than the total stopping distance, factoring in sensor pipeline latency, transport jitter, and state estimation uncertainty. Furthermore, powered deceleration requires electrical bus energy and closed-loop control authority to survive an upstream fault. Logic-level power alone cannot generate mechanical braking torque.

The intent lease defines the temporal horizon over which a deliberative goal remains valid. It operates alongside the chunk lease of @sec-nervous-lease-sizing rather than replacing it, because the two hold different kinds of authority even though the Safety MCU's permission path checks both. The chunk lease authorizes motion. It allows an admitted chunk to drive the actuators only for its short lease unless the chunk policy renews it at its own rate. By contrast, the intent lease authorizes a goal, fixing which target that motion may pursue, how hard it may press, and until when, and only newer evidence can renew it. Consequently, each lease ends authority from its own side. When the chunk lease lapses, motion stops even though the goal remains valid. When the intent lease lapses, nominal tracking toward the goal ends at once, even if the current chunk still has lease time left, and the MCU engages the validated fallback (@sec-planning-handoff-record). A rejected proposal is the gentler case, because it revokes nothing and leaves already admitted motion running until its own leases lapse. The physical stopping budget must accommodate the cumulative delay across perception, communication, actuator response, and mechanical braking in every case.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_latch_stall_force_ladder.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Three orange bars on a log scale against a red dashed vertical line labeled 100 newtons limit. A tripwire bar of 15 newtons and an at-brake bar of 39 newtons end left of the line; a bar for a 200 millisecond stall reaches 2,400 newtons, far past it."}

*A `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_stall_arm_str` unbraked stall drives the latch to `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_unbounded_n_str`, far past its limit.*
:::

::: {#nbk-intent-lease-duration-collision-exposure-tradeoff-across .callout-notebook title="What the latch ceilings buy"}

**Problem**: The intent lease for the cage door requests a `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_trip_str` tripwire and a `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.v_latch_str` approach speed against a `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_lim_str` latch limit. With the local contact loop in place, what force does the latch see when the brake command issues, and what would it see in a counterfactual design with no local contact trip, where pressing stops only when the proposer or the intent lease acts?

**Variables**:

- Tripwire `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_trip_str` and approach speed $\LatchApproachSpeed =$ `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.v_latch_str`, the requested ceilings; latch limit `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_lim_str` (Illustrative)
- Plate stiffness $\LatchPlateStiffness =$ `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.k_latch_str` (Illustrative) and contact-loop response `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_contact_str`
- Unbraked stall $\FiniteChange \MonotonicClockInstant =$ `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_stall_arm_str` (Illustrative), shorter than one `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_intent_period_str` intent period

**Math**:

1. **Force at brake command**: The tripwire fires at `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_trip_str`, and the plate keeps compressing while the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_contact_str` contact loop responds, so the force when the brake command issues is $\BrakeCommandForce = \ContactTripwireForce + \LatchPlateStiffness\,\LatchApproachSpeed\,\ContactLoopResponseTime =$ `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_trip_str` $+$ `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.k_latch_str` $\times$ `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.v_latch_str` $\times$ `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_contact_str` $=$ `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_at_brake_onset_n_str`. The arm stop that follows has only a fraction of a millimeter of compression left to spend; @sec-enforcement-intentional-contact derives that stop (@eq-release-trip-indentation).
2. **Stall travel** (counterfactual, no local trip): $\FiniteChange \ApproachPosition = \LatchApproachSpeed\,\FiniteChange \MonotonicClockInstant =$ `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.v_latch_str` $\times$ `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_stall_arm_str` $=$ `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.delta_x_unbounded_mm_str` past first contact.
3. **Stall force**: $\LatchStallForce = \LatchPlateStiffness\,\FiniteChange \ApproachPosition =$ `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.k_latch_str` $\times$ `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.delta_x_unbounded_mm_str` $=$ `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_unbounded_n_str`.

**Result**: The contact loop brakes at `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_at_brake_onset_n_str`. Without the local trip, a stop that waited on the proposer would let the arm press on, and the spring model predicts `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_unbounded_n_str`.

**Systems insight**: The predicted force lies far past the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_lim_str` limit, beyond the point where the spring model applies at all; the latch has failed. Sizing and arresting transient contact within milliseconds is the duty of the high-rate, low-latency contact loop. The intent lease supplies the operational boundaries (velocity caps and force tripwires) that keep dynamic loads within the contact loop's braking envelope, ensuring physical safety even when upstream deliberative proposers stall across multiple intent cycles.
:::

Both the mug grasp and the latch engagement depend on a **privilege separation boundary**\index{Privilege separation!intent boundary}.[^fn-ai-subsumption-intent] While deliberative models propose goal targets and operational bounds, an independent supervisor enforces safety invariants and executes certified fallback maneuvers whenever evidence expires or contact states change unexpectedly. This design decouples deliberative reasoning from real-time physical protection, inverting the classical priority hierarchy found in early reactive control systems [@brooks1986robust].

[^fn-ai-subsumption-intent]: **Subsumption Architecture**\index{Architecture!subsumption}\index{Control!subsumption}: In the classic subsumption architecture of @brooks1986robust, a higher layer subsumes a lower one by suppressing its inputs or inhibiting its outputs. Physical AI systems invert that priority. The lower, real-time layer retains absolute veto authority over deliberative proposals because its timing, stability, and failure behavior can be strictly bounded.

Structured intent handoffs explicitly disentangle task tolerance, sensor uncertainty, actuator effort limits, and fallback trajectories. External dynamic processes, however, dictate how long these static bounds remain valid. On a moving conveyor, for instance, a correctly localized workpiece drifts continuously after perception capture. The mathematical model governing this uncertainty growth establishes the strict temporal deadline that the independent safety controller must enforce.

## Expiring Goals and Temporal Validity Leases {#sec-intent-goals-expire}

Suppose the host application processor hangs while the robotic arm reaches for the red mug on the moving belt. The fault that makes canceling the reach necessary is the very fault that prevents a cancellation command from being sent. An explicit abort requires a working sender, scheduler, and network link, while the belt carries the mug beyond the grasp tolerance regardless of when the model last published a coordinate. An intent lease must therefore expire autonomously from the physics of environmental drift. Autonomous expiry applies the third law, proposal is not permission (principle \ref{pri-vol4-proposal-permission}), to physical goals, so that the permission side and not the proposer decides when authority ends. In distributed systems, Gray and Cheriton [-@gray1989leases] introduced leases to maintain cache consistency: a coordinator grants time-bounded authority that lapses unless explicitly renewed, preventing a crashed client from blocking others indefinitely. That correctness proof assumes bounded clock drift between client and coordinator. In an embodied system, the Safety MCU enforces this assumption by transforming every incoming timestamped epoch into its own local monotonic timebase with a strictly bounded synchronization error. The physical domain raises the stakes, because an expired cache lease merely delays a read, whereas an unexpired motion lease lets moving mass keep consuming physical clearance unchecked. The privileged Safety MCU acts as coordinator, issuing a transient tracking lease to the unprivileged deliberative host. If the host stalls during inference, pauses for garbage collection, or experiences an operating system kernel panic, the Safety MCU's local hardware countdown expires and automatically engages a validated fallback response. This requires no network packet or cancellation command from the failed host.[^fn-hw-watchdog-rtt]

Lease duration is measured exclusively against the Safety MCU's monotonic hardware clock.[^fn-monotonic-clock-lease] Network time-synchronization daemons or operator adjustments can step wall-clock time abruptly backward or forward, while host-level software watchdogs can freeze alongside the user-space process they are designated to monitor. Furthermore, no inference pipeline, regardless of its mean throughput, completely eliminates long-tail p99 scheduling stalls. Placing the lease countdown on an isolated, hardware-timed MCU counter ensures that target authority is revoked locally the instant the lease expires. This hardware isolation decouples expiry detection from host operating system jitter, although total physical stopping distance must still account for fieldbus transmission, drive response, and kinematic deceleration.

[^fn-monotonic-clock-lease]: **Monotonic Clock**\index{Clock!monotonic}: A counter that only advances forward at a fixed nominal rate, such as POSIX `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` or a free-running microcontroller timer. A lease evaluated against wall time could gain or lose its entire remaining window in a single clock adjustment. Every measurement in this chapter is therefore evaluated on the Safety MCU's monotonic counter and converted from external clocks with a bounded synchronization error.

The deadline the lease enforces is the evidence horizon $\EvidenceHorizon$ of @sec-brain-two-proposers put to a new use. There it bounded how long the evidence behind a chunk keeps the tracked mug within tolerance (@eq-brain-evidence-horizon). Here the intent lease\index{Evidence horizon!intent lease} starts from the same quantity, and memory supplies its value. The mug-handle belief record carries an invalidation horizon $\BeliefInvalidationHorizon$ (@eq-mem-invalidation-horizon), the elapsed time before its error growth law (@eq-mem-occlusion-expansion) reaches the task tolerance. The lease reads that horizon with the grasp tolerance $\PositionalTaskTolerance$ as the error ceiling and the initial sensor error $\InitialTrackingError$ as the starting bound.

For a conveyor pick, the growth law charges two bounded effects against that ceiling:
$$\PositionErrorBound(\FiniteChange \MonotonicClockInstant) = \InitialTrackingError + \DriftVelocityBound\,\FiniteChange \MonotonicClockInstant + \tfrac{1}{2}\,\SlipAccelerationBound\,\FiniteChange \MonotonicClockInstant^2$$ {#eq-intent-evidence-growth}
Here $\DriftVelocityBound$ bounds the relative velocity between the gripper frame and the target, including both conveyor motion and unmodeled mobile-base odometry drift, and $\SlipAccelerationBound$ bounds the residual slip acceleration of the mug on the belt. The evidence-only horizon is the elapsed time at which $\PositionErrorBound(\FiniteChange \MonotonicClockInstant)$ reaches $\PositionalTaskTolerance$. The numerical examples in this chapter evaluate this upper ceiling with zero additional controller tracking reserve. An admission gate, however, must first subtract a separately qualified nonnegative scalar tracking reserve from $\PositionalTaskTolerance$. It then solves @eq-intent-evidence-growth against the reduced budget. It refuses immediately if the initial target error plus that reserve already reaches the tolerance (alongside the full 3D error-set containment check of @sec-intent-lease). The two limiting regimes are horizons derived earlier in the volume. With no tracker, the horizon is the linear horizon of @eq-mem-linear-horizon, with belt speed as its growth rate. With a tracker that cancels belt velocity, the horizon is the slip-only root of @eq-brain-evidence-horizon. In this chapter's symbols they read
$$\UntrackedEvidenceHorizon = \frac{\PositionalTaskTolerance - \InitialTrackingError}{\DriftVelocityBound} \quad (\SlipAccelerationBound = 0), \qquad \TrackedEvidenceHorizon = \sqrt{\frac{2(\PositionalTaskTolerance - \InitialTrackingError)}{\SlipAccelerationBound}} \quad (\DriftVelocityBound = 0)$$ {#eq-intent-evidence-horizon-roots}
These evidence-only roots are upper ceilings on target lifetime. When drift velocity and slip acceleration act together, $\EvidenceHorizon$ is the positive root of $\PositionErrorBound(\FiniteChange \MonotonicClockInstant) = \PositionalTaskTolerance$ in @eq-intent-evidence-growth, which is strictly shorter than either single-effect root.

[^fn-hw-watchdog-rtt]: **Watchdog Timer**\index{Hardware!watchdog timer}: An independently clocked down-counter that forces a hardware reset or a safe fallback output unless software reloads it before reaching zero. Because a crashed host cannot reload it, the lease countdown runs on the isolated Safety MCU rather than in the host process it supervises.

If $\PositionalTaskTolerance \le \InitialTrackingError$, the target is inadmissible at the moment of perception. Initial measurement uncertainty alone consumes the entire task tolerance, which obligates the safety controller to reject dependent motion commands immediately. Even when the evidence horizon is strictly positive, granting motion permission requires a separate geometric verification. The system must verify that current physical clearance accommodates total sensing latency, permission evaluation time, fieldbus transmission delay, mechanical brake engagement, and physical braking distance.

For a red mug carried on a takeaway conveyor, the untracked linear root dictates the evidence deadline. Sizing the control pipeline requires determining whether deliberative intent models can refresh targets rapidly enough to renew authority before this window elapses. While the evidence-horizon calculation in @sec-brain-two-proposers sized the low-level chunk execution policy against this horizon, deliberative intent models evaluate on a substantially slower cycle.

::: {#nbk-intent-cadence-gap .callout-notebook title="The cadence gap"}

**Problem**: The conveyor carries the mug at `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.v_conveyor_str`. Can the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_intent_str` intent model keep the target inside its tolerance by re-proposing it, and how slowly would the belt have to run for a model-only renewal to suffice?

**Variables**:

- Grasp tolerance $\PositionalTaskTolerance =$ `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.r_tol_str` and initial handle error $\InitialTrackingError =$ `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.e0_str` (Illustrative)
- Belt speed $\DriftVelocityBound =$ `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.v_conveyor_mm_str` (Illustrative)
- Intent period $\IntentProposalPeriod =$ `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_intent_period_str` (Chosen, `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_intent_str`) and inference $\ProposerInferenceTime =$ `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_intent_infer_str` (Derived, @sec-brain-memory-wall)

**Math**:

1. **Horizon** (@eq-intent-evidence-horizon-roots): with no tracker, $\EvidenceHorizon = \UntrackedEvidenceHorizon =$ (`{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.r_tol_str` $-$ `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.e0_str`) $/$ `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.v_conveyor_mm_str` $=$ `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_untracked_str`.
2. **Error at one period**: `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.e0_str` $+$ `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.v_conveyor_mm_str` $\times$ `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_intent_period_str` $=$ `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.err_at_period_str`, `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.err_excess_str` past the tolerance. Inference alone overruns the horizon by `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_intent_infer_str` $-$ `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_untracked_str` $=$ `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_infer_overrun_str`.
3. **Renewal ceiling**: Each model-only renewal installs a target computed from a frame captured one inference earlier, and that target stays in force until the next renewal replaces it one period later. Just before the replacement, the evidence behind it is $\IntentProposalPeriod + \ProposerInferenceTime =$ `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_renew_age_str` old (the reaction latency of @sec-brain-action-chunking, here for the intent model), so the drift it can keep up with is (`{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.r_tol_str` $-$ `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.e0_str`) $/$ `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_renew_age_str` $=$ `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.v_renew_max_str`.

**Result**: The model alone could renew the target only on a belt running at `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.v_renew_pct_str` percent of its speed. Even a slow settling drift of `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.v_drift_slow_str`, such as a mug still sliding to rest after the belt stops, whose `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_slow_drift_str` horizon is charted against inference latency in @fig-10-lease-dynamics-tradeoff, is too fast for it.

**Systems insight**: Physical drift and allowable tolerance dictate $\EvidenceHorizon$, independent of computing performance. An intent renewal can extend operational authority only if the sum of its dispatch period and inference latency fits entirely within this window. Artificially inflating the lease duration to cover inference delay leaves the pose estimate outside its declared tolerance envelope for `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_infer_overrun_str`. Without a qualified, high-frequency local tracker, the system must either slow or stop the conveyor, or refuse the pick task entirely.

:::

The `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_untracked_str` limit is a physical evidence deadline that only fresh sensor observations, validated against current motion, can extend. Faster deliberative inference does not lengthen this physical evidence horizon, although a sufficiently fast capture-to-admission pipeline and renewal cadence can fit inside it.

Deploying a qualified local tracker changes these dynamics. By re-measuring the mug in every camera frame and matching conveyor velocity, the local tracking loop prevents conveyor speed from driving error growth. While the initial perception uncertainty of `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.e0_str` still counts against the grasp tolerance, it leaves a target-only error margin of `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.err_budget_str` for unmodeled physical perturbations before reserving controller tracking error. Sizing against an illustrative worst-case residual slip acceleration of `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.a_slip_str`, this remaining margin yields the same `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_tracked_str` tracked horizon that @sec-brain-two-proposers computed for the chunk policy. Because the local tracking pipeline runs at high frame rates, only the tracker's brief period plus sensing latency must fit within this expanded horizon. The tracker also changes who renews the lease. Each tracked frame yields a newer belief record of the same handle, and the producer re-proposes the same referent against it. The Safety MCU therefore receives renewals with a newer capture epoch on the tracker's cadence rather than the model's. Relieved of geometric tracking, the deliberative intent model only re-confirms semantic identity (which mug to grasp) at its own rate, and no renewal waits for a fresh inference. The lease attaches its target to the handle's affordance frame, whose base-frame pose under a qualified tracker follows the belt. The goal set therefore moves with the mug. The tolerance bounds only how far the handle departs from the tracked estimate under residual slip, rather than how far it departs from a fixed point in the base frame. Whichever horizon governs the active operating mode caps the duration of the intent lease granted for that target (@sec-intent-lease).

Examining a host processor stall illustrates the protection each horizon provides. Suppose the robotic arm reaches toward the red mug under a target admitted without local tracking, and the application processor stalls during neural network inference. If the system held that unvalidated target across a `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_stall_intent_str` stall, the actual mug position would drift `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.err_stalled_untracked_str` away from the commanded setpoint, causing the gripper to close on empty air or strike the rim. The Safety MCU does not rely on host health to catch this fault. In the ideal zero-additional-reserve case, at `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_untracked_str` the lease expires automatically, commanding braking to begin within `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_arm_onset_str` (accounting for one permission evaluation tick, one fieldbus cycle, and actuator brake onset), even if the current chunk's own lease has time left. In contrast, under a qualified local tracker, an identical `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_stall_intent_str` stall leaves the target estimate displaced by only `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.err_stalled_tracked_str`, inside the target-only tolerance budget, because the ideal tracked horizon extends to `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_tracked_str`. Delegating fast geometric updates to local tracking is what allows a `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_intent_str` deliberative intent model to operate safely in a dynamic physical environment.

On one clock, the proposer's timing loses to both horizons (@fig-10-mug-lease-timeline). Both idealized zero-additional-reserve countdowns end before the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_intent_infer_str` inference returns and well before the next proposal at `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_intent_period_str`, so the model can renew neither lease. Absent other renewals, each expiry is followed by the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_arm_onset_str` stop onset. Under a qualified tracker the tracked countdown restarts with every tracked frame, long before it reaches `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_tracked_str`, so the tracked bar in the figure shows what happens only when those renewals stop, as they do when the host stalls. What follows that expiry is still motion, as panel (b) of @fig-10-intent-lease-envelope sketches in speed against time. The drive begins braking `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_arm_onset_str` after expiry, and the stopping distance under the falling curve must already fit the clearance that remains. This is why the lease carries the stopping deadline as a term of its own (@sec-intent-lease).

::: {#fig-10-mug-lease-timeline fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Mug lease against the intent model's timing**: The top lane charges the conveyor mug's modeled target error against the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.r_tol_str` grasp tolerance. Without tracking, belt speed exhausts it at `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_untracked_str`; with a tracker that cancels belt velocity, residual slip exhausts it at `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_tracked_str`. The bottom lane puts idealized countdowns with zero additional controller reserve on the Safety MCU's clock beside the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_intent_infer_str` inference and the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_intent_period_str` proposal period; each expiry is followed by the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_arm_onset_str` stop onset (hatched). Neither lease can wait for the next proposal. After a `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_stall_intent_str` host stall the untracked target sits `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.err_stalled_untracked_str` off and the tracked one `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.err_stalled_tracked_str`." fig-alt="Two stacked panels sharing a time axis from 0 to 560 milliseconds. Top: target error in millimeters against time. A dashed bronze line rises from 3 millimeters and crosses a dashed 15-millimeter tolerance line at 60 milliseconds; a solid teal curve crosses it at 219 milliseconds. Square markers at 200 milliseconds mark 43 and 13 millimeters. Bottom: three rows. An intent-model bar ends at 336 milliseconds, with a marker for the next proposal at 500 milliseconds. Two idealized zero-additional-reserve lease bars end at 60 and 219 milliseconds, each followed by a hatched 22-millisecond stop-onset segment."}

```{python}
#| label: plot-intent-mug-lease-timeline
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ MUG LEASE AGAINST THE INTENT MODEL'S TIMING (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-10-mug-lease-timeline
# │
# │ Goal:    show why the 2 Hz intent model cannot renew an untracked conveyor
# │          target and what a tracker buys.
# │ Show:    target error vs. time (untracked 60 ms, tracked 219 ms, 15 mm
# │          tolerance, 43/13 mm after a 200 ms stall); lease countdowns with
# │          the 22 ms stop onset beside 336 ms inference and the 500 ms period.
# │ How:     reads calc-intent-lease-duration-collision-exposure; no literals.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from mlsysim import viz
from mlsysim.core.units import millisecond, millimeter
from mlsysim.fmt import check

# ┌── 1. LOAD (values from calc-intent-lease-duration-collision-exposure) ─────
E0 = AISLE.grasp_initial_error.to(millimeter).magnitude  # category: illustrative (aisle scenario)
R_TOL = AISLE.grasp_tolerance.to(millimeter).magnitude  # category: illustrative (aisle scenario)
V_BELT = AISLE.v_conveyor.to(millimeter / millisecond).magnitude  # mm per ms
A_SLIP = AISLE.a_conveyor_slip.to(millimeter / millisecond**2).magnitude  # mm per ms^2
T_UNTR = tau_ev_untracked.to(millisecond).magnitude
T_TRK = tau_ev_tracked.to(millisecond).magnitude
T_INFER = RM.intent_inference_latency.to(millisecond).magnitude
T_PERIOD = t_intent_period.to(millisecond).magnitude
T_STALL = delta_t_stall_intent.to(millisecond).magnitude
T_ONSET = t_arm_onset_after_expiry.to(millisecond).magnitude
ERR_STALL_U = err_stalled_untracked.to(millimeter).magnitude
ERR_STALL_T = err_stalled_tracked.to(millimeter).magnitude

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
t = np.linspace(0, 560, 800)
err_untracked = E0 + V_BELT * t
err_tracked = E0 + 0.5 * A_SLIP * t**2
check(abs(np.interp(T_UNTR, t, err_untracked) - R_TOL) < 1e-6, "untracked curve crosses the tolerance at tau_ev")
check(abs(E0 + 0.5 * A_SLIP * T_TRK**2 - R_TOL) < 1e-6, "tracked curve crosses the tolerance at tau_ev,tracked")
Y_TOP = 50.0

# ┌── 3. PLOT ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
R = viz.VOL4_ROLES
viz.set_book_style()
fig, (ax, bx) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.6, 4.6), sharex=True, gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [1.35, 1.0], "hspace": 0.08})
for a in (ax, bx):
    a.tick_params(labelsize=9)
    a.grid(False)
    for s in ("top", "right"):
        a.spines[s].set_visible(False)

# Top lane: modeled target error against the grasp tolerance.
ax.axhspan(R_TOL, Y_TOP, color=R["consequence"], alpha=0.07, lw=0, zorder=0)
ax.axhline(R_TOL, color=R["consequence"], lw=1.3, ls=(0, (5, 3)), zorder=2)
ax.text(552, R_TOL + 1.2, f"grasp tolerance $r_{{\\mathrm{{tol}}}}$ = {R_TOL:.0f} mm", ha="right", va="bottom", fontsize=9, color=R["consequence"])
ax.plot(t, np.minimum(err_untracked, Y_TOP + 5), color=R["proposal"], lw=2.0, ls=(0, (6, 2)), zorder=4)
ax.plot(t, np.minimum(err_tracked, Y_TOP + 5), color=R["measured"], lw=2.2, zorder=4)
ax.text(150, 41, "untracked (belt speed)", fontsize=9, color=R["proposal"], ha="right", va="center")
ax.text(322, 23, "tracked (residual slip)", fontsize=9, color=R["measured"], ha="left", va="center")
# Horizons
for tx, col in ((T_UNTR, R["proposal"]), (T_TRK, R["measured"])):
    ax.plot([tx], [R_TOL], "o", ms=5.5, color=col, zorder=6)
    ax.vlines(tx, 0, R_TOL, color=col, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (1, 2)), zorder=3)
ax.text(T_UNTR + 6, R_TOL - 1.2, f"$\\tau_{{\\mathrm{{ev}}}}$ = {T_UNTR:.0f} ms", fontsize=9, color=R["proposal"], ha="left", va="top")
ax.text(T_TRK + 5, 1.2, f"$\\tau_{{\\mathrm{{ev,tracked}}}}$ = {T_TRK:.0f} ms", fontsize=9, color=R["measured"], va="bottom")
# Stall points
ax.vlines(T_STALL, 0, Y_TOP, color=R["neutral"], lw=0.8, ls=(0, (3, 3)), zorder=1)
ax.plot([T_STALL], [ERR_STALL_U], "s", ms=5, color=R["proposal"], zorder=6)
ax.plot([T_STALL], [ERR_STALL_T], "s", ms=5, color=R["measured"], zorder=6)
ax.text(
    T_STALL + 6,
    ERR_STALL_U,
    f"{ERR_STALL_U:.0f} mm",
    ha="left",
    va="center",
    fontsize=9,
    color=R["proposal"],
    bbox=dict(boxstyle="square,pad=0.08", fc="white", ec="none"),
    zorder=7,
)
ax.annotate(
    f"{ERR_STALL_T:.0f} mm",
    xy=(T_STALL, ERR_STALL_T),
    xytext=(T_STALL - 45, 24),
    ha="center",
    va="center",
    fontsize=9,
    color=R["measured"],
    zorder=7,
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=R["measured"], lw=0.7, shrinkB=3),
)
ax.text(T_STALL - 5, Y_TOP - 1, f"host stalled {T_STALL:.0f} ms", ha="right", va="top", fontsize=9, color=R["neutral"])
ax.set_ylim(0, Y_TOP)
ax.set_yticks([0, E0, R_TOL, 30, 45])
ax.set_ylabel("target error (mm)", fontsize=9)

# Bottom lane: ideal zero-additional-controller-reserve countdowns on the MCU clock.
rows = {"intent model": 2.0, "untracked ceiling": 1.0, "tracked ceiling": 0.0}
H = 0.5

def tint(hex_color, a):
    h = hex_color.lstrip("#")
    return tuple(1 - a * (1 - int(h[i : i + 2], 16) / 255) for i in (0, 2, 4))

bx.broken_barh([(0, T_INFER)], (rows["intent model"] - H / 2, H), facecolor=tint(R["proposal"], 0.22), edgecolor=R["proposal"], lw=1.0)
bx.text(T_INFER / 2, rows["intent model"], f"inference {T_INFER:.0f} ms", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=9, color="#1A202C")
bx.plot([T_PERIOD], [rows["intent model"]], marker="v", ms=6.5, color=R["proposal"], zorder=5)
bx.text(T_PERIOD - 9, rows["intent model"], f"next proposal {T_PERIOD:.0f} ms", ha="right", va="center", fontsize=9, color=R["proposal"])
for name, tx in (("untracked ceiling", T_UNTR), ("tracked ceiling", T_TRK)):
    y = rows[name]
    bx.broken_barh([(0, tx)], (y - H / 2, H), facecolor=tint(R["structural"], 0.18), edgecolor=R["structural"], lw=1.0)
    bx.broken_barh([(tx, T_ONSET)], (y - H / 2, H), facecolor=tint(R["consequence"], 0.15), edgecolor=R["consequence"], lw=1.0, hatch="////")
    bx.plot([tx, tx], [y - H / 2 - 0.08, y + H / 2 + 0.08], color=R["consequence"], lw=1.6)
    bx.text(tx + T_ONSET + 8, y, f"expiry {tx:.0f} ms, stop onset +{T_ONSET:.0f} ms", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=9, color="#1A202C")
bx.set_yticks(list(rows.values()))
bx.set_yticklabels(list(rows.keys()), fontsize=9)
bx.tick_params(axis="y", length=0)
bx.set_ylim(-0.55, 2.55)
bx.set_xlim(0, 560)
bx.set_xlabel("time since capture (ms)", fontsize=9)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.17, right=0.98, top=0.98, bottom=0.11)
plt.show()
```

![](images/svg/fig10_lease_dynamics_tradeoff.svg){width="100%"}
